paras: The reported threatened lynching of Arthur Burton followed his arrest at Brownsville, Linn County, Oregon, in June 1888, when Burton, described as "a mulatto," was charged with raping Eliza Harrington, a girl of about sixteen. A condensed regional news column said Burton escaped lynching only through the efforts of his guard, and the story was reprinted in Idaho papers in July. Brownsville's own correspondent called the report of an attempted lynching "without foundation," and no report of the outcome of the case was found.

The Albany State Rights Democrat described Burton as "a mulatto aged about eighteen" and a brother-in-law of Minor Jackson of Brownsville. Harrington, about sixteen, had been living with her aunt, Mrs. Ziner.

According to the girl's account as printed in Albany, Burton entered her room on a Friday night, told her he would kill her if she made any noise, chloroformed her and assaulted her. He was arrested the following Monday and on Tuesday was taken before Squire Averill, where he waived examination and was held under $1,000 bonds. Unable to give bond, he was brought to Albany by Constable S. P. Barger, "for safe keeping" in the words of the Brownsville correspondent of the Lebanon Express.

The State Rights Democrat reported that "great excitement prevailed in Brownsville over the affair." The same report said the girl was confined to her room and was said to be out of her mind at least part of the time, both then and before the night in question. Burton, for his part, said he was innocent and would "come out all right."

Shortly before June 26, Harrington was examined as to her sanity before Justice Humphrey and a board of physicians and was discharged as not insane, according to the Albany Herald as quoted in the Salem Evening Capital Journal. The Herald expected the case of the state against Burton to come up in circuit court that week. At Brownsville, ex-Sheriff George Humphrey was reported summoning witnesses for the grand jury, and Harrington left for Albany in the company of Deputy Sheriff Humphrey. In July the Linn County commissioners allowed $14 in fees for her examination. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict was found.

The Linn County papers treated the case cautiously. The State Rights Democrat said there were "two sides to the case" and refrained from comment so as not to prejudice it, while adding that if the charge proved true "there is no punishment too severe for the offense." The Lebanon Express's Brownsville correspondent wrote that "the most exaggerated reports have gained circulation," that public opinion was divided on Burton's guilt, and that the town was willing to await a fair trial.

The lynching story came instead from a condensed "Oregon News" column printed on another page of the same June 29 issue of the Lebanon Express. That brief identified Burton as "a mulatto," called Harrington "his victim" and her assailant "her ravisher," and so presented the charge as fact. The column ran unchanged in the Mountain Home Bulletin on July 7 and the Idaho Semi-Weekly World on July 10.

Accounts conflict on whether Burton faced a lynching threat at all. The regional brief said he "only escaped being lynched by the strenuous exertions of his guard," while the Brownsville correspondent said the report of an attempted lynching "is without foundation." The denial came from the town itself, and the earlier Albany report described excitement but no mob. The papers also differ on smaller points: the brief named the magistrate Justice Avery rather than Averill, and the correspondent called the accused "Albert" Burton.

reader.title: Reported threatened lynching of Arthur Burton
bases: A regional news brief reported that Burton, jailed on a rape charge, narrowly escaped being lynched (A6); the Brownsville correspondent denied any attempted lynching (A5), so the episode is at most a reported, contested lynching threat.

Burton was not killed; he was held in jail and his case went toward the grand jury (A2, A3, A5). The only report of a lynching threat names no crowd or mob (A6) and is denied by the local correspondent (A5).

The arrest and charge are reported by several independent papers (A2, A3, A5, A6), but the lynching threat appears only in the 'Oregon News' brief and its reprints (A6, A8, A9) and is explicitly called 'without foundation' by the Brownsville correspondent (A5).

accounts.label: Albany local report
accounts.gist: Burton arrested on the girl's complaint, waived examination and was jailed at Albany; great excitement at Brownsville, but the girl's mental state was in question and there were 'two sides to the case'. No lynching threat mentioned.

accounts.label: Regional 'Oregon News' brief
accounts.gist: Burton, 'a mulatto', committed the outrage after chloroforming the girl; amid much indignation he escaped lynching only by his guard's exertions.

accounts.label: Brownsville correspondent
accounts.gist: Nothing beyond floating reports was known since Burton waived examination; opinion was divided, exaggerated reports circulated, and the attempted-lynching report was without foundation.

framing.detail: The State Rights Democrat refrained from comment because of 'two sides to the case' but said that if true 'there is no punishment too severe for the offense'.
The Lebanon Express's Brownsville correspondent stressed divided opinion and 'exaggerated reports' and denied the lynching story, citing the town's willingness to await a fair trial.
The condensed 'Oregon News' column called Harrington 'his victim', her assailant 'her ravisher', and reported the near-lynching; reprinted in two Idaho papers.
